summary.text: Viscosity is a property of a fluid that measures how strongly it resists force when one part of it moves relative to another.
For liquids it matches the everyday idea of thickness, so syrup has a higher viscosity than water.
In liquids it comes from cohesive molecular forces, while in gases it comes from molecular collisions.

facts.label: Everyday meaning
facts.value: For liquids, thickness: syrup beats water

facts.label: SI units
facts.value: Pascal-seconds, or newton-seconds per square metre

facts.label: Zero viscosity
facts.value: Seen only in superfluids at very low temperatures

items.prompt: To push syrup through a tube at a steady rate, you must keep pushing. What is that push mainly working against?

options.label: Friction between layers of the fluid that are moving at different speeds
The weight of the tube pressing on the syrup
Air pressure squeezing the syrup from outside
The syrup slowly turning into a solid

items.explain: A force is needed to overcome friction between fluid layers in relative motion, and that force is proportional to the viscosity.

items.prompt: What makes the resistance to flow in a liquid different from that in a gas?

options.label: In a liquid it comes from molecules colliding, in a gas from attraction between them
In a liquid it comes from attraction between molecules, in a gas from molecules colliding
Both come from molecules colliding, but liquids collide more often
Gases have none at all, because their molecules are too far apart

items.explain: In liquids viscosity arises from cohesive molecular forces, while in gases it results from molecular collisions.

items.prompt: Two people drag a spoon through the same bowl of water. One drags it slowly, the other quickly, over the same distance. Who feels more resistance?

options.label: The slow one, because the spoon spends longer in the water
Neither, because the distance is the same
The quick one, because the resistance depends on how fast the shearing happens
The slow one, because the water has time to cling to the spoon

items.explain: In a fluid like water, stresses from shearing do not depend on how far it was sheared but on how quickly the shearing occurs.

items.prompt: An engineer wants a pump fluid with no internal friction at everyday temperatures. Is that possible?

options.label: Yes, any gas has no viscosity at room temperature
Yes, if the fluid is purified enough
No, but only because every liquid is thicker than water
No, because every fluid has some viscosity except superfluids at very low temperatures

items.explain: Zero viscosity appears only in superfluids at very low temperatures. Otherwise all fluids have positive viscosity.

items.prompt: A lab tech measures the same oil's resistance to flow when it is cold and when it is warm, and the numbers differ. Why?

options.label: Viscosity depends on a fluid's state, including its temperature
Viscosity is a fixed property of each liquid and cannot change
The oil's resistance to flow changes only when it is poured faster
Only gases change their resistance to flow with temperature

items.explain: Viscosity depends on a fluid's state, such as its temperature, pressure and rate of deformation.

items.prompt: Viscosity is a force multiplied by a time and divided by an area. Which SI unit does that give?

options.label: Newtons per second
Pascals per metre
Pascal-seconds
Joules per second

items.explain: Force times time over area gives newton-seconds per square metre, also called pascal-seconds.
